title: Notes on a Musical Staff
description: Read the basic page symbols used to place a melody on five lines.
cardDescription: Read the basic page symbols used to place a melody on five lines.
focus: The staff locates pitches; a clef gives those lines and spaces their note-name reference.
solvingTip: Start with the shapes visible on the printed page.
words: Set of five parallel lines used for musical notation
Symbol setting the pitch reference of a musical staff
Word before clef for the familiar curled G-clef symbol
Word before line for a short extra line beyond the staff
Gap between two neighboring staff lines
One of the five parallel marks in a staff
Symbol representing a musical sound and its duration
Thin upright stroke attached to many printed notes
Oval part of a printed musical note
Word before clef for the symbol often used for low notes
Symbol that raises a written note by a semitone
Symbol that lowers a written note by a semitone
Symbol canceling a written sharp or flat
How high or low a written note sounds

answerNotes.STAFF: Notes can be placed on lines or in the spaces between them.
answerNotes.CLEF: A clef gives meaning to note positions rather than setting the tempo.
answerNotes.TREBLE: Treble clef places G on the second line of the staff.
answerNotes.LEDGER: Ledger lines extend notation above or below the five main lines.
answerNotes.SPACE: A note in a space has a different position from a note on a line.

title: Counting a Simple Musical Beat
description: Follow note lengths, silent rests, and the steady pulse beneath a familiar tune.
cardDescription: Follow note lengths, silent rests, and the steady pulse beneath a familiar tune.
focus: In common four-four counting, a quarter note often represents one beat; other meters use different conventions.
solvingTip: Use counting words before the printed notation terms.
words: Steady underlying beat felt in a piece of music
Note value often counted as one beat in four-four time
Note value half as long as a quarter note
Symbol marking a period of musical silence
Device clicking or marking a steady practice beat
Note value lasting twice as long as a quarter note
Note value lasting four quarter-note durations
Mark adding half the original value to a note's duration
Thick line joining the stems of short note values
Say numbers to keep track of a musical pulse
At a low speed, as a practice tempo may begin
At a high speed, as a lively tempo may be
Mark a steady pulse with a finger or foot
One regular pulse unit in the music

answerNotes.PULSE: A pulse is the regular reference, while rhythms can move across it.
answerNotes.QUARTER: The count depends on the meter; a quarter note is not always one beat.
answerNotes.EIGHTH: Two eighth notes equal one quarter note in written duration.
answerNotes.REST: A rest has a duration just as a sounded note does.
answerNotes.METRONOME: A metronome supplies a reference pulse, not the melody.

title: Major, Minor, and Musical Steps
description: Explore simple scale words through intervals, starting notes, and familiar keyboard directions.
cardDescription: Explore simple scale words through intervals, starting notes, and familiar keyboard directions.
focus: Major and minor describe scale structures; their emotional effect is not identical in every piece.
solvingTip: Short direction and distance words help cross the scale terms.
words: Ordered sequence of musical pitches moving up or down
Starting and home note of a musical key
Interval between one C and the next C above it
Smallest step between neighboring piano keys in standard tuning
Scale type whose common forms include a lowered third
Scale type with a characteristic whole-step and half-step pattern
Small movement from one scale note to the next
Group of pitch relationships centered on a tonic
Foundational note used to name a chord
Distance in pitch between two musical notes

answerNotes.SCALE: A scale is a sequence, unlike a chord whose notes may sound together.
answerNotes.TONIC: The tonic serves as a reference point for the key.
answerNotes.OCTAVE: Notes an octave apart share a letter name but differ in pitch.
answerNotes.SEMITONE: A semitone may connect two white keys or a white and black key.
answerNotes.MINOR: Minor has several forms, so not every minor scale uses the same notes.

title: Loud, Soft, and Shaping a Phrase
description: Identify basic expression marks that guide a musician's loudness and the way notes connect.
cardDescription: Identify basic expression marks that guide a musician's loudness and the way notes connect.
subtheme: Loud, Soft, and Shaping a Phrase
focus: Dynamics concern loudness, while articulation describes how notes begin, end, or join.
solvingTip: The familiar loudness words can help with the Italian directions.
words: Musical term for changes and levels of loudness
Direction to play notes smoothly connected
Direction to play notes short and detached
Emphasis placed on a particular note
Quiet in volume, as a gentle passage is
Strong in volume, as a forceful passage is
Curved notation mark joining notes into a smooth group
Short musical idea shaped as a unit
Increase and sometimes ease back in musical loudness
Quality of sound shaped by the performer

answerNotes.DYNAMICS: Dynamics differ from tempo, which concerns speed.
answerNotes.FORTE: Forte indicates a dynamic level rather than a fast tempo.
answerNotes.PIANO: Piano is a loudness direction here, not the keyboard instrument.
answerNotes.CRESCENDO: A crescendo changes loudness over a passage rather than instantly.
answerNotes.LEGATO: Legato concerns connection rather than a fixed volume.

title: Finding Your Place in Sheet Music
description: Navigate the measure numbers, repeat marks, and ending directions of a simple printed score.
cardDescription: Navigate the measure numbers, repeat marks, and ending directions of a simple printed score.
subtheme: Finding Your Place in Sheet Music
focus: A repeat sign sends a player back to a marked point; an ending bracket shows which passage to take on a repeat.
solvingTip: Start with the page-navigation words you recognize.
words: Group of beats between neighboring bar lines
Direction to play a marked passage again
Vertical mark separating measures, two words
Passage under a numbered bracket in repeated music
Italian word marking the end in some musical directions
Concluding section reached by a marked musical direction
Printed symbol guiding a jump or return in the score
One side of a printed sheet of music
Move to the next page while following a score
Printed identifier helping locate a particular measure
Place where a musical passage begins
Three-letter word before segno in the direction to return to a sign
Word after da in the direction to return to the beginning
Written music showing one or more parts

answerNotes.MEASURE: A measure organizes beats according to the time signature.
answerNotes.REPEAT: A repeat applies to a defined passage rather than necessarily the entire piece.
answerNotes.BARLINE: Bar lines divide measures and do not by themselves indicate a pause.
answerNotes.ENDING: First and second endings let repeated sections finish differently.
answerNotes.FINE: Fine means the ending point in this context, rather than a judgment of quality.
